Thanks for the clear list. Attached is a concise playbook (PDF) and our latest Q2 DR test spreadsheet; below are the high-level answers you can paste into the RFP. Laura (SE) and Dev (SRE) are looped in for any deep dives.

High-level RTO / RPO (typical targets):
- Hosted API (Redwood cloud):
  - RTO: automated regional failover for API routing: target < 60s for new requests (transparent routing to healthy region).
  - RPO: persistent customer data (logging, audits, user-provided storage) = 0 (durable to external object stores); in-memory KV cache for session acceleration = best-effort, typical RPO < 30s for active sessions unless customer persists session state.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity):
  - RTO: warm-standby and cross-region routing enabled; target 5–15 minutes for capacity failover when using Redwood-managed image snapshots and warm nodes (depends on config).
  - RPO: configurable — with continuous replication of control-plane metadata, target RPO < 1 minute for control-plane items; in-memory session caching same as Hosted.
- Private / VPC / On-prem:
  - RTO: depends on customer infra and runbook; recommended architecture for 1-hour RTO: active-passive across regions with automated DNS routing + IaC templates.
  - RPO: depends on customer-managed persistence; Redwood supports synchronous replication to customer-managed object stores where required.

Automatic vs manual failover:
- Hosted: routing and health checks in the control plane are automated. If a whole region is unreachable, traffic is routed to the next healthy region by policy. Most API-level reconnections are automatic; per-tenant circuit-breakers and canary routing can be configured for conservative failover.
- Dedicated: we offer automated routing if warm-standby is enabled; otherwise initial remediation is automated (node restart, image swap) and full capacity failover can be manual (operator-driven) depending on contract.
- Private: by default manual (customer-run) unless we operate a managed private control plane.

Failback and data consistency:
- Failback is performed after the source region is verified healthy. For Hosted, we recommend a staged failback: 1) resume routing to primary for a small percentage of traffic, 2) monitor telemetry and logs for 24–72 hours, 3) do full cutover. Persistent data (object stores) maintains consistency; for in-memory session caches, we recommend session reconciliation or client-side session tokens to rehydrate state.

In-memory KV cache handling:
- KV cache is considered ephemeral acceleration layer. We provide best-effort prefix caching with optional export hooks to persist session state to object storage or a customer-managed Redis. If you require zero loss for session state, we recommend integrating an external durable store as part of the architecture.

DR test cadence and evidence:
- Tabletop exercises: quarterly.
- Automated regional failover test (Hosted): quarterly partial failovers, annual full-region simulation.
- Dedicated/Private: test cadence agreed per contract (typical: semi-annual full failover).
- Attached spreadsheet contains Q2 test results: simulated regional outage (partial failover), average RTO observed, and issues discovered.

Attachments: 2026-08-03_Redwood_GeoRedundancy_Playbook.pdf, RTO_RPO_Test_Results_Q2_2026.xlsx

Aaron —

Answered inline below, and included a short checklist at the end you can drop into the RFP annex.

1) In-flight requests during Hosted failover:
- Typical behavior: if routing is switched mid-generation, the client will usually get a truncated response or an error depending on where the model was in the generation pipeline. We implement idempotent request tokens and recommend clients retry with the same request token. For critical flows we recommend streaming checkpoints or using our explicit persist API to flush intermediate state.

2) Dedicated reserved + warm-standby operational steps:
- Warm nodes: pre-provisioned VMs/GPU instances kept in a ready state with warmed model caches.
- Automatic: health checks detect primary failure -> traffic is diverted via smart routing to standby region; if additional capacity is needed, autoscaling policies (pre-warmed) expand within 2–10 mins depending on instance availability.
- Manual: ops will trigger capacity rebalancing using our control plane; manual steps typically take 15–45 minutes for large capacity shifts and are documented in the runbook.

3) Private deployment customer-run checklist (short):
- Verify DNS TTLs are set to <= 60s for rapid failover.
- Pre-provision certificates for both primary and DR regions; include automated cert issuer where possible.
- Ensure network ACLs and firewall rules are mirrored ahead of time; test connectivty to storage endpoints.
- IaC templates (Terraform/CloudFormation) available to reprovision nodes quickly.
- Verify backup snapshot cadence (nightly) and point-in-time restore windows.

Tabletop report: we have a 1-page summary suitable for procurement. I attached a redacted tabletop summary PDF to the Drive link and included a short excerpt in the attachment 'Redwood_GeoRedundancy_Playbook.pdf'.

Checklist excerpt you can paste: 
- Target RTO (Hosted): < 60s for new requests; RTO for in-flight request recovery: best-effort, client retry recommended.
- Target RPO (Hosted): persistent data = 0; ephemeral caches = < 30s typical.
- DR test cadence: Hosted quarterly partial failovers, annual full-region simulation.
- Recommended private architecture: active-passive across regions, Terraform templates, DNS TTL <=60s.
